'''''Luffa aegyptiaca''''', the '''sponge gourd''',<ref>{{PLANTS|id=LUAE|taxon=Luffa aegyptiaca|accessdate=23 June 2015}}</ref> '''Egyptian cucumber''' or '''Vietnamese luffa''',  is an [[Annual plant|annual]] species of [[vine]] cultivated for its fruit, native to [[South Asia|South]] and [[Southeast Asia]].

== Description ==

The three-lobed [[leaves]] are {{Convert|7.5-20|cm|abbr=off|frac=2}} wide.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |title=The Complete Guide to Edible Wild Plants |publisher=[[Skyhorse Publishing]] |others=[[United States Department of the Army]] |year=2009 |isbn=978-1-60239-692-0 |location=New York |pages=117 |language=en-US |oclc=277203364}}</ref>

The fruit, approximately {{Convert|30|cm|abbr=on}} long and maturing to brown, resembles a [[cucumber]]<ref name=":0" /> in shape and size.

== History ==
=== Etymology ===

The synonymous botanical [[specific epithet (botany)|specific epithet]] "''aegyptiaca''" was given to this plant in the 16th century when European botanists were introduced to the plant from its cultivation in Egypt. In the European botanical literature, the plant was first described by [[Johann Veslingius]] in 1638, who named it "Egyptian cucumber". Veslingius also introduced the name "Luffa".<ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=uNsbiJt7bQ4C&pg=PA48 Johann Veslingius, ''De Plantis Aegyptiis'', 1638. p. 48 (in Latin)]</ref>

== Varieties == 
=== Cultivars in North America ===

== Uses ==
[[File:Luffa aegyptiaca (5).jpg|thumb|Cooked luffa]]
=== Culinary ===

The young fruit is eaten as a vegetable and is commonly grown for that purpose in tropical Asia. The young shoots, flowers and leaves can be cooked, and the mature seeds can be roasted for consumption.<ref name=":0" />

=== Sponge ===

Unlike the young fruit, the fully ripened fruit is strongly fibrous and inedible, and is used to make scrubbing [[bath sponge]]s. Due to the use as a scrubbing sponge, it is also known by the common names '''dishrag gourd''', '''rag gourd''', '''sponge gourd''', and '''vegetable-sponge'''.<ref name=grin/> It is also called '''smooth luffa''' to distinguish it from the ridged luffa (''[[Luffa acutangula]]''), which is used for the same purposes.<ref name=grin/>

=== Oil extract ===

An edible oil can be extracted from the seeds. The resulting oil meal can be fed to [[rabbit|rabbits]] and [[catfish]], or used as a fertilizer.<ref>Heuzé V., Tran G., Lebas F., 2017. Luffa (Luffa aegyptiaca). Feedipedia, a programme by INRA, CIRAD, AFZ and FAO. https://www.feedipedia.org/node/626 Last updated on July 18, 2017, 10:53</ref>

=== Art ===
In the Levant, ''Luffa aegyptiaca'' has been in use since late antiquity. Young fruits were used for food. Mature fruits were used as bath sponges. Roman mosaics featuring ''Luffa aegyptiaca'' fruits have been discovered in churches and synagogues throughout [[Palestine]].

== Cultivation ==
Luffa has been cultivated throughout Asia for centuries for use as a household cleaning agent and is now, due to the gently abrasive quality of the natural fibers, a popular exfoliating agent in the eco-friendly cosmetic industry.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=Luffa Gourds |url=http://agsyst.wsu.edu/LuffaGourds.html |access-date=2022-10-20 |website=Washington State University Extension}}</ref> Owing to its striking yellow flowers, the plant is occasionally grown as an ornamental.

=== Climate ===
It requires much heat and a lot of water to thrive.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Davis |first=Jeanine M. |date=1994-04-01 |title=Luffa Sponge Gourd Production Practices for Temperate Climates |url=https://journals.ashs.org/hortsci/view/journals/hortsci/29/4/article-p263.xml |journal=HortScience |language=en-US |volume=29 |issue=4 |pages=263–266 |doi=10.21273/HORTSCI.29.4.263 |issn=0018-5345|doi-access=free }}</ref>
However, ''Luffa aegyptiaca'' can be cultivated in temperate climates. Research from North Carolina suggests that commercial production of luffa in the United States could be economically viable.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Davis |first=Jeanine |date=December 12, 2018 |title=Commercial Luffa Sponge Gourd Production {{!}} NC State Extension Publications |url=https://content.ces.ncsu.edu/commercial-luffa-sponge-gourd-production |access-date=2022-10-18 |website=content.ces.ncsu.edu |language=en-US}}</ref>

=== Growth ===
Techniques that contribute to success in growing luffa include using black mulch to warm soil temperatures and transplants to increase the germination rate and extend the growing season. Narrow spacing may result in poorer quality sponges.<ref name=":2" /> It is best grown with a [[Trellis|trellis]] support for its curled [[tendril]]s to hang on to.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.gardenguides.com/396-legacy-luffa.html|url-status=unfit|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201130145415/http://www.gardenguides.com/396-legacy-luffa.html|archive-date=2020-11-30|date=2017-09-21 |title=A Legacy of Luffa|first=Elizabeth|last=Harwick|website=Garden Guides|quote=growing ''Luffa cylindrica'' successfully in South Carolina.}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.thespruce.com/luffa-plant-profile-4796761 |title=How to Grow and Care for Luffa|date=2022-04-05 |access-date=2023-04-18 |website=[[The Spruce]] |last=Hassani|first=Nadia|publisher=[[Dotdash Meredith]] |author-link=Nadia Hassani|editor-last=Harris|editor-first=Sonya|editor-link=Sonya Hassani|publication-place=[[New York City|New York]]|language=en-US |format=HTML |quote=A trellis like those used for cucumbers and pole beans works well [...] add string in a V-pattern so the tendrils of the vines have something to grab onto. |ref=toc-luffa-care}}</ref>
